books.t: Wind and Truth (The Stormlight Archive, #5)
books.rev:
Wow. Can’t believe I’m finished with the first arc of the Stormlight archive. This is probably my least favorite book of the five (my favorite is Words of Radiance), but I still liked it a lot and had lots of fun reading it throughout the past month. 

Yes it’s long but it didn’t feel like 1300+ pages. The whole book felt like a Sanderlanche, with an extra Sanderlanche towards the end. 

Great audiobook narration by Michael Kramer and Kate Reading as always.

I think all the criticisms about this book are totally valid. Gods showing up at the end and telling people what to do. Kaladin becoming a therapist when it felt like he was going to become the bringer between singers and humans. Etc etc. BUT, I trust Brandon Sanderson and all those stuff that people complain about didn’t really annoy me because I thought the ending was great and all the characters are left off in places that totally make sense for a 10 year time jump between the books and finished off their arcs.

books.t: An African History of Africa: From the Dawn of Humanity to Independence

books.t: Montaigne
books.rev:
After only reading 2 books by Stefan Zweig, he is slowly becoming one of my favorite authors. 

I love that Zweig focuses more on the psychological aspects of the people he chooses to write about and what drove them to do what they did, rather than listing all the events in their life. 

Zweig wrote this book shortly before killing himself in Brazil, and with very little access to his library,  he gives a rundown of Montaigne's life and how he remained free during times of civil war. He shares parallels to his own life relating his experiencet during he Nazi regime to Montaigne's almost 400 years before during times of civil war in France. The introduction to this book where he talks about that topic is fun to read.

I picked this book up because of a couple of reasons:
1. My mom's aunt recommended me to read Montaigne's Essays
2. Ryan Holiday bought 1000 copies (all the available stock) of this book to prevent it from going out of print because of how much he loves this book
3. It cost me 2 usd on Kindle because of a daily deal lol

books.t: The Strength of the Few (Hierarchy, #2)
books.rev:
James Islington knows how to write a great ending!! Unlike many other reviews, I didn’t find it slow or boring. I was engaged in most parts of the book, except for Obetium, where the only interesting character was Careor, who disappeared halfway through. I also enjoyed Lucuem throughout the book, but I found his friends in Loch Trenala dull. But it makes sense considering the limited time we spent with them and the world-building required for the new world. It didn’t have the same tension that made The Will of The Many hard to put down.

I spoiled most of the book because I was reading theories on Reddit, which revealed that Callidus and his family would return and that Ruarc was Careor in Lucuem. Initially, from reading the spoilers I was scared of how it was going to be handled and was prepared for the worst, but James Islington’s execution handled it extremely well. Curious to see what death really means and if one can actually die forever. Because characters like Amhose and his father came back to life and died again, curious to know if they remain dead or they can be revived again. It’s one of those books where I don’t care about the characters, and I’m reading it to see where the plot ends up. I think the world and magic system James Islington has built is incredible.

I enjoyed The Will of the Many more, but I’m very excited the rest of the series! I was confused on whether I liked how James Islington wrote/his writing style in the first book, but now I’m a fan. I can’t wait for The Justice of One!

3.7!!!!

books.t: Empire of Silence (The Sun Eater, #1)
books.rev:
I love first-person books. I hadn't read one where the main character is writing a memoir about his life, and I love it. I seriously think this has the potential to be one of my favorite series of all time. I didn’t find it slow or boring at all, unlike many people. The moments that others found boring, I found interesting because of how Hadrian narrates and reflects. I did a combination of immersive reading and listening to the audiobook while walking around Madrid. The narrator is great. His tone of voice does a great job at encapsulating Hadrian's melodramatic personality. Christopher Ruocchio is a great writer. He does a great job of painting an image of what the world looks like. I can't wait to read the rest of this series. 

I also think this has one of the best opening lines to a book I've read. We're straight up told how it's going to end on the first page, and it leaves us wondering how Hadrian blew up a sun? And especially in this book, it left me wondering just that.

books.t: The Will of the Many (Hierarchy, #1)
books.rev:
Very conflicted on what to think and rate. I'm giving it 3.7, might bring it up to 4 later, as I feel that I'm sometimes too generous with my ratings.

I loved all the history behind the auorae culamne, the cataclysm, and the magic system (literally draining the will and drive out of people) is interesting and exciting.

It took me a long time to get into this book, not because of the pacing (which I thought was good) but because it just wasn't my vibe, and I desperately wanted to read something else. For almost a week, I didn't read it because I was bored with it, and I almost DNFed it. However, I had heard many good things about the second half of the book, so I stuck with it and binged it over the past 4 days (because I wanted to get it over with to start The Empire of Silence), and I ended up reading 85% of it during that time and enjoyed it. 

Vis is just good at everything to the point where it's annoying and OBVIOUS he is going to succeed. And I didn't really care about any of the characters, but not in a negative way; I just remained neutral. Except for maybe Callidus. One thing I liked about the characters is that I love how they were introduced. 

The ending and the plot twist were CRAZY and unexpected. I want to read The Strength of The Few sooo bad (but I'm prioritizing The Wheel of Time and Suneater). I had fun reading the last half and had to sit up straight several times. I liked the writing. I'm excited to see where James Islington is going to take this series, as I thought it does a GREAT job of setting the groundwork for the whole series. And I'll probably be reading The Licanius Trilogy sometime soon. I'm very excited to see where this series goes. I overall had lots of fun. But I do think that book influencers hyped this book up a lot.

Also, feels WAY too much like Red Rising

I'll be reading book 2 because of that ending and because I’ve heard it’s 3 times better if you know what I mean 🤣🤣🤣

books.t: Animal Farm

books.rev:
Great book. It was way better than I expected. I had bought this book with an Audible credit almost a year ago. I remember I had started it and didn't get past the 2nd chapter because I didn't understand what was going on. I decided to leave it for a later date. I’m glad I did that, I wouldn’t have appreciated this book for what it was if I had read it then. 

I enjoyed the perspective it was narrated from. It was this weird combination of third-person limited and omniscient, while following Dorian Gray most of the time. The first half of the book switches perspectives a couple of times, and then it locks into Dorian. I liked it a lot because it helps you understand the other characters better. The version I read gave a short introduction to Oscar Wilde and the book. It was great having that introduction since it gave context for the whole book. Most of those introductions in other books are boring, but this one was good. The introduction makes me want to read De Profundis!!. The book itself was great. Great narration from Ben Barnes. It's crazy to me that this was written in 1890. 

I had started reading this book a while ago, but never marked it as "currently reading." I finished the last part while walking around Busan!!

The characters (specially Bilbo!!), the wittiness of the dialogue (for example, Gandalf asking Bilbo about what he means by “good morning”), Tolkiens descriptiveness of the surroundings, and even the POV from which we read/are told the story from gave me a warm, whimsical, and cozy feeling.

books.t: Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals
books.rev:
A great book that most of us should read. It'll be like a slap in the face for most people.

"The average human lifespan is absurdly, terrifyingly, insultingly short. Here’s one way of putting things in perspective: the first modern humans appeared on the plains of Africa at least 200,000 years ago, and scientists estimate that life, in some form, will persist for another 1.5 billion years or more, until the intensifying heat of the sun condemns the last organism to death. But you? Assuming you live to be eighty, you’ll have had about four thousand weeks. Certainly, you might get lucky: make it to ninety, and you’ll have had almost 4,700 weeks." - Burkeman, Oliver. Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals (p. 3).

We will never have time to accomplish everything. Even though we humans were given the ability to accomplish anything, we lack the necessary time to do so.

I thought it was a nice and refreshing perspective on productivity!

books.t: Piranesi
books.rev:
Incredible writing and does a great job at conveying a magical, soothing, and whimsical feeling. I read this without knowing anything about it other than that it was about a house with tides, I didn’t even read the blurb (and still haven’t). I recommend you do the same if you are thinking of reading this book.

It’s one of those books where you could spend hours thinking about and analyzing its meaning. But just like Piranesi said to the other in one part of the book, maybe it’s a riddle that isn’t meant to be unraveled.

I’ve seen lots of reviews say that it’s more of a slow atmospheric book, and I agree. For the first couple chapters it seems like nothing is really happening (it ends up important because it’s scene setting) and we’re reading Piranesi’s journal entries, and then towards the end it picks up. 

I enjoyed this book a lot. I ended up only reading a few pages the first couple days I started reading this and didn’t get that hooked. But once I got on the plane I couldn’t stop reading. I read both the kindle and audiobook at the same time. The narrator is brilliant.

The book overall is a completely different vibe from the other Stormlight books, and the purpose of this book is to expand the world and fill in gaps for Lift and another character (which is why you should read this between Oathbringer and Words of Radiance). For the first half of Edgedancer, we follow Lift causing trouble, stealing food, and annoying her spren that she calls voidbringer.

Some parts were kind of boring, but I had fun. I also loved the last line of the book lol.

books.t: The Rise of Rome (The Great Courses)
books.st: The Rise of Rome (The Great Courses)
books.rev:
I wish I could absorb everything about this book. History is sooo interesting, and reading just one book about the formation of Rome to the fall of the Roman Republic isn't enough to fully understand and grasp it.

I love how it's not just a Rome encyclopedia of names and dates, but actually tells you about the important historical figures and the normal, day-to-day life of its inhabitants.. The lecturer/professor does a great job at not boring you with historical facts and makes it entertaining. I tried listening to another audiobook from The Great Courses about the history of India, but I had to DNF it because it was boring (nothing to do with the history of India itself, which I find fascinating). I enjoyed that he gave multiple theories for certain events that occurred. 

I love history!! Now it's time to listen to Gregory Aldrete on Lex Fridman's podcast.

Magellan's achievement is extraordinary, but his life’s work was sadly diminished into a simple historical fact and almost forgotten.The route to the spice islands through the Strait of Magellan, or beneath Patagonia, didn’t turn into the great trading route that Magellan had imagined. And the spice islands that he conquered for Spain with the price of his life were sold back to Portugal a couple years later.

This translation wasn't the best. I wanted to buy the Eden Paul and Cedar Paul version, but this one was on Kindle Unlimited so I read it. The first 70 pages was a tough read, and I almost DNFed it because I wasn’t liking the translation and was reading it just to finish it. But after that, it got way better and I actually enjoyed reading the rest of it. I don’t think the translation and writing improved in the later pages, but I just got hooked on the Magellan’s life instead.

If you’re interested in history and Magellan’s life specially, then I recommend this book.

books.t: Words of Radiance (The Stormlight Archive, #2)
books.rev:
This is the highest rated book on GoodReads, and it completely lives up to that expectation. I listened to the whole book because I'm a good Vorin man (lol). The Sanderlanche hit while I was walking on the road/sidewalk and it had me jumping around and punching the air, and if a book has me doing that in public then it did something right. The whole book had me in a trance from the very the prologue’s very first word. For 14 days, I didn't want to do ANYTHING but read this book. It was on my mind 24/7. To the point that it had me repeating Kaladin's ideals while paddling out to catch a wave during a surfing session because the waves kept falling on me hahahaha.

“Honor is dead, I’ll see what I can do” had tears forming in my eyes. One of the best things I’ve read along with when he bonds with Syl again

This book is Shallan's book, we see her flashbacks instead of any other characters (in The Way of Kings it was Kaladin's flashbacks) and I loved her as a character way more than the first book. She has real stakes and her flashbacks reveal many of her past actions and why the people around her did the things they did (iykyk). I also thought she was more likeable in general, the fact that she was forced to grow as a person because of  Jasnah’s death definitely had a contributing factor to that. In book 1, everytime a Shallan chapter was next I groaned and really wanted to skip it (up until the end), and this book had me excited for Shallan's chapters and had me wondering what she was doing whenever we were looking at another POV. Adolin is another character that comes into the spotlight in this book for me. In the first book, he just felt like Dalinar's son. But in Words of Radiance he's more than that. And Kaladin... is one of my favorite character in the whole series (Wit, lopen, and dalinar are close as well), and probably of fiction in general. Kaladin's arc in this book is incredible.  From discovering his powers and beating the shit out everyone in the 4v1 and the Szeth 1v3, to almost killing Syl (adhd tinkerbelle) and losing his powers, to regaining the powers because he finally has the balls to do/see what is "right" in his eyes, regaining the bond with Syl, and flying (or falling lol) into the center of the shatterplains and basically saving the day and killing Szeth.  I have no clue what is going to happen in the future books, and I’m excited to see what is made of these characters.

This is a book that automatically enters my favorite list, and it got a 5 stars in my eyes way before it ended. I love Sanderson's prose, dialogue, action scenes, the cliffhangers at the end of each part and POV change, the worldbuilding (even though the interludes sometimes seem useless, they add soo much to the world because you feel like things other than what the MCs are doing are going on, the mythology, religions, and creatures make the scale of the world huge), the magic system is easy to understand with clear rules set in place, he's great at foreshadowing events (for example, when the stormfather said one of her daughters was disobeying him, I instantly knew it was Syl bonding with Kaladin again, the stakes are real, and the characters feel real because they aren’t perfect.

I wish this 1000+ page book and 50 hour audiobook was longer.

books.t: Wanting: The Power of Mimetic Desire in Everyday Life
books.rev:
Before reading this book, I didn't think someone could write a book on desire. A YouTube video is enough, right? I was wrong. 

This book is incredible. I consider it a must-read, especially now that we've never had so much access to the amount of mimetic models we have today. This book will help you become more conscious of how mimetic desire is affecting your life. 

I could have finished this book in a couple of days, but I’m glad it took me over two weeks. It allowed me plenty of time to reflect on it.

Yeah, it follows the same formula as most self-help books (I personally don't have a problem with it):
1. Introduction to the concept
2. Story
3. Touches back on the concept again
4. Repeat

And you could probably find many flaws if you're reading it to critique, you'll find them. But if you look beyond that and focus on the concept, then this is a great book.

books.t: The Death of Ivan Ilych
books.rev:
I've been wanting to read this book for a long time, and now that I'm reading more fiction, I saw it as the perfect opportunity to read it.

The Death of Ivan Ilyich is a book about a man who lives a life that's very respectable on the surface. He lives without questioning anything and follows the path laid out for him because that's what everyone else is doing. And then death appears to him...

"‘What if I really have been wrong in the way I’ve lived my whole life, my conscious life?’ It occurred to him that what had once seemed a total impossibility – that he had not lived his life as he should have done – might actually be true. It occurred to him that the slight stirrings of doubt he had experienced about what was considered good by those in the highest positions, slight stirrings that he had immediately repudiated – that these misgivings might have been true and everything else might have been wrong. His career, the ordering of his life, his family, the things that preoccupied people in society and at work – all of this might have been wrong. He made an attempt at defending these things for himself. And suddenly he sensed the feebleness of what he was defending. There was nothing to defend."

"But more dreadful than the physical pain was the suffering in spirit, his greatest agony."

"Julius Caesar is a man, men are mortal, therefore Caesar is mortal–had always seemed to him to be true only when it applied to Caesar, certainly not to him. There was Caesar the man, and man in general, and it was fair enough for them, but he wasn’t Caesar the man and he wasn’t man in general, he had always been a special being, totally different from all others" "Yes, Caesar is mortal and it’s all right for him to die, but not me, Vanya, Ivan Ilyich, with all my feelings and thoughts–it’s different for me. It can’t be me having to die. That would be too horrible."

"Don’t ever take 'can’t' as the answer unless you’ve verified that it is against the law or against the laws of physics. People told me I can’t legally own property. The agent said I can’t buy it for such a cheap price. They were wrong."

"Bad luck sometimes just falls in our laps no matter what we do, so they expect good luck to do that too. From everything I’ve read and grown ups I’ve talked to, good luck almost never works like bad luck. Good luck requires us to do something on purpose to earn it. We either have to make sure we’re ready to use it when it does come, or go out looking for it."

books.t: The Conquest of Happiness
books.rev:
I started to read this book because I was thinking of the turkey induction problem, where a turkey is fed daily by a farmer, and since he is fed daily, he expects this pattern to continue forever. But, on Thanksgiving Day, the farmer cuts the turkey's neck instead of feeding it. I asked ChatGPT what book the turkey induction problem came from, and it said this book. So I read it, thinking I was going to find it, but I quickly realized I had chosen the wrong book. Either way, this book is a great read. This book is very different from other self-help books about happiness, which give you "the 10 steps to a happy life." Instead, it assumes you're the ordinary day-to-day person who suffers from unhappiness, from which most people suffer and helps you understand why you are unhappy and ways to deal with it (without giving you a formula or steps on how to become happy). If you're generally an unhappy person, then I recommend this book.

I'm a very happy person, so I already did, consciously or unconsciously, the stuff mentioned in this book. Reading it was like having someone put into words the things I’d already figured out through experience.

"One should respect public opinion insofar as is necessary to avoid starvation and keep out of prison, but anything that goes beyond this is voluntary submission to an unnecessary tyranny."

“The secret of happiness is very simply this: let your interests be as wide as possible, and let your reactions to the things and persons that interest you be as far as possible friendly rather than hostile.”

You'd think that this book would just be pure physics and stories about it, but I was wrong. Richard Feynman was one of those people who was interested in and would do everything from cracking safes in Los Alamos, selling art, endless pranks, and even joining a Brazilian Bongo group in Rio. It seemed that he just followed his curiosity wherever it took him without caring about what others thought. He seems like the type of guy who starts doing something because why not. 

Also, I think the book's subtitle, "Adventures of a Curious Character," perfectly describes this book.

books.t: I Don't Want To Grow Up: Life, Liberty, and Happiness. Without a Career. (Nature Book Series)
books.st: I Don't Want To Grow Up
books.rev:
This book is for a very specific type of person: the person who doesn’t want to conform within the standard of society. The others, may not enjoy it as much and will think it’s just this rich white guy taking advantage of his “privileges” (I don’t think that, but some people who have read this book do. Look at the reviews lol). 

Not growing up is completely different than what we have been told it is, and this book helps you understand what that really means. 

“What does it mean to grow up? Many things, to be sure. For me, it has always meant giving up on your dreams and facing reality. But whose reality? When we're young, we have dreams as big as the world.
Then, when we're older, we're told to face reality— as if our dreams and reality are in direct conflict.”

“Refusing to grow up is choosing to live-and experiencing every day with the playfulness and curiosity of a child. When we stop seeing the world as a playground, nature as a classroom, beauty in the mundane—we perish.”

- quotes from the book. 

The book is a part memoir and part self-help. It turned out to be more self-help than I thought it was going to be, which isn’t a bad thing, but I didn’t read this book with the intention of reading self-help. However, the lessons resonated with me a lot because they were things I was thinking about before reading the book (following the breadcrumbs, nudges, etc.).

It’s nothing ground breaking or new for me. It’s pretty short (120 pages) and an easy read. But it was a fun reas and time well spent.

books.t: Jung: A Very Short Introduction
books.rev:
A couple of months ago, when I was in Bali, I went to a dream interpretation workshop. The lady who gave the workshop was based on Jung's ideas. It was a great workshop and I learned a lot. After the workshop, I went up to talk to her, and I realized I hadn’t read any psychology books (apart from Flow and a body language book), even though I owned many. Ever since then, I've had the urge to read Jung. And a couple of days ago, this book was on sale on Kindle. So I bought it!

The book was short and a great introduction to Carl Jung and his ideas. I was familiar with some of his ideas, but it was just surface-level stuff. This is still kind of surface-level, but it gives you back story and goes more in-depth compared to what I knew before. I would recommend this book to people who want to get into Jungian psychology or are just curious. It's a short book, but not a quick read,

books.t: Stolen Focus: Why You Can't Pay Attention— and How to Think Deeply Again
books.rev: Stolen Focus is a must-read. It approaches the topic of our decreasing attention spans differently compared to other books on this topic, for example: Indistractable. Indistractable says it’s an individual problem, that it’s our fault our attention spans are like this, and we must fix it. Stolen Focus says it’s not our fault. Jonathan Hari says, “Every time we turn off our phones, we have 1000 engineers working against us.” This book also discusses individual solutions, but it mostly talks about solutions we must make as a society, like changing the business models of social media platforms and how childhood trauma causes ADHD. It’s a great book that goes perfectly with The Anxious Generation by Jonathan Haidt. It has a whole chapter dedicated to the transition of play-based childhood to phone-based and its effects. Both of these books are must-reads in my opinion. This book will help you understand a lot of things from this subject, not only why we are losing attentions but how and why they are doing it. I listened to it as an audiobook, and it was a great listen.

"IT WAS MAY 14. In a few days my class back in Jamestown, North Dakota would be graduating from high school, and I was in Singapore."

But, the book turned out to be something entirely different. It's about Louis L'Amour and all the different jobs he had throughout the world, the people he met, and the books he read.

books.t: The Universe and the Teacup: The Mathematics of Truth and Beauty

I was in the waiting area of the Dehradun airport waiting to board a plane heading to Mumbai. To pass the time, I was reading Freedom from the Known by J. Krishnamurti when a guy walked past and noticed I was reading a book. He ducked down to see what book I was reading and gave me a thumbs up. A couple of minutes later, the same guy passed by and gave me The Universe and the Teacup. He said he was glad to see me reading Krishnamurti, and he thought that I might like this book about math. I was so confused but so happy at the same time.

I didn't end up reading the book until a month later. I read it because one day I woke up with the urge to read it after not having thought about the book in a while. I ended up liking the book!. books.t: Steve Jobs
books.rev: Steve Jobs might have been a pain in the ass, but without a doubt, he was a genius. Being a pain in the ass and his sociopathic tendencies were what led to Apple’s, Pixar’s, and NeXT’s success. His life was fascinating, from his insane diet to him abandoning his child and how that was similar to his childhood and even how he ran Apple. He literally changed entire industries. It is a brilliant book; I loved it. This book definitely inspired me. I can’t wait to read Walter Issacson’s other biographies. I would have loved to see what he would have made if he were still alive.

books.t: When Breath Becomes Air
books.rev: Paul was an excellent writer. This book is an excellent reminder that death is inevitable, and we don't know when it'll come. We plan our lives assuming that we will live for 70+ years, but in reality, who knows if we will make it. I think Paul's life was a perfect example of this. He has worked all his life to become a neurosurgeon, which consists of long hours of work and training. He did it all thinking about what he would be doing five years down the line, and that future got taken away from him. The epilogue was heartbreaking. I plan to listen to the audiobook version of this book soon. I love memoirs and biographies!!!
